verses.text: After Moses, the LORD's servant, died, the LORD spoke to Joshua son of Nun, who had served as Moses' assistant.
“My servant Moses is dead. Now get up and cross the Jordan with all these people into the land I'm giving the Israelites.
I've given you every place your feet will touch, just as I told Moses.
Your territory will stretch from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great Euphrates River, across all the Hittite country and west to the great sea, where the sun goes down.
Nobody will be able to stand against you as long as you live. I'll be with you just as I was with Moses. I won't fail you or abandon you.
Be strong and brave. You'll lead these people into the land I swore to give their ancestors as an inheritance.
Be strong and very brave. Make sure you live by every part of the law my servant Moses gave you. Don't turn away from it to the right or to the left, so things will go well wherever you go.
Keep the words of this book of the law on your lips. Think about them day and night, so you'll carefully do everything written in it. Then you'll prosper on your way and succeed.
Haven't I told you to be strong and brave? Don't be afraid or lose heart. The LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”
Then Joshua gave orders to the people's officers.
“Go through the camp and tell everyone, ‘Get your food ready. Within three days you'll cross the Jordan and take possession of the land the LORD your God is giving you.’”
Joshua spoke to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh.
“Remember what Moses, the LORD's servant, told you: ‘The LORD your God is giving you rest and will give you this land.

Your wives, your children, and your livestock will stay in the land Moses gave you on this side of the Jordan. But all your brave fighting men are to cross over armed ahead of your fellow Israelites and help them

until the LORD gives them rest, just as he gave you rest, and they take possession of the land the LORD your God is giving them. Then you can go back and settle in your own land, the land Moses, the LORD's servant, gave you east of the Jordan.’”
They answered Joshua, “We'll do everything you've commanded us, and we'll go wherever you send us.
We'll listen to you in everything, just as we listened to Moses. May the LORD your God be with you as he was with Moses.
Anyone who rebels against your orders and refuses to listen to what you command will be put to death. Just be strong and brave.”
Joshua son of Nun secretly sent two men from Shittim to scout the land. “Go look over the land, including Jericho,” he told them. They went to the house of a sex worker named Rahab and stayed there.
Word reached the king of Jericho: “Some Israelite men came here tonight to scout the land.”
The king sent Rahab a message: “Bring out the men who came into your house. They're here to spy on the whole country.”
But Rahab had taken the two men and hidden them. She said, “Yes, the men came to me, but I didn't know where they were from.
They left after dark, around the time the gate was closing. I don't know where they went. If you hurry after them, you might catch them.”
In fact, she'd taken them up to the roof and hidden them beneath the flax stalks she'd spread out there.
The king's men chased them along the road toward the crossings of the Jordan. As soon as the men left, the city gate was shut.
Before the two men lay down to sleep, Rahab came up to them on the roof.
She said, “I know the LORD has given you this land. We're terrified of you, and everyone who lives here is losing heart because of you.

We heard how the LORD dried up the waters of the Red Sea in front of you when you came out of Egypt. We also heard what you did to Sihon and Og, the two Amorite kings across the Jordan, whom you completely destroyed.
As soon as we heard, our hearts sank. Nobody had any courage left to face you, because the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on earth below.
So please swear to me by the LORD that, since I've shown you kindness, you'll also show kindness to my father's family. Give me a sign I can trust.
Spare my father, my mother, my brothers, my sisters, and everyone who belongs to them. Save us from death.”
The men told her, “Our lives for yours, as long as you keep quiet about what we're doing. When the LORD gives us the land, we'll be kind to you and keep our word.”
Then she lowered them by a rope through the window, because her house was built into the city wall and she lived there.
She said, “Head for the hills so the men chasing you won't find you. Hide there for three days until they've come back. Then you can go on your way.”
The men said, “Here are the conditions of the oath you had us swear.
When we come into the land, tie this scarlet cord in the window you lowered us through. Bring your father, mother, brothers, and your whole family into the house with you.

If anyone goes out of your house into the street, they'll be responsible for what happens to them, and we'll be clear of blame. If anyone lays a hand on someone inside the house with you, we'll answer for it.
But if you tell anyone what we're doing, we'll be released from the oath you had us swear.”
“Agreed,” she said. She sent them on their way, and after they left she tied the scarlet cord in the window.
The men went into the hills and stayed there three days until the men chasing them had returned. Their pursuers searched all along the road and never found them.
Then the two men came down from the hills, crossed the river, and returned to Joshua son of Nun. They told him everything that had happened.
They said to Joshua, “The LORD really has handed the whole land over to us. Everyone who lives there is losing heart because of us.”
Joshua got up early, and he and all the Israelites left Shittim and came to the Jordan. They camped there before crossing.
After three days, the officers went through the camp.
They told the people, “When you see the Levitical priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, leave where you are and follow it.
Keep about two thousand cubits between you and the ark. Don't get any closer. That way you'll see where to go, since you've never been this way before.”
Joshua told the people, “Set yourselves apart for God, because tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you.”
Joshua told the priests, “Pick up the ark of the covenant and cross ahead of the people.” They picked it up and went ahead of everyone.
The LORD told Joshua, “Today I'll begin to honor you in front of all Israel, so they'll know that I'm with you just as I was with Moses.
Tell the priests carrying the ark of the covenant, ‘When you reach the edge of the Jordan, step into the river and stand still.’”
Joshua told the Israelites, “Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God.”
He said, “Here's how you'll know that the living God is among you and will certainly drive out the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites ahead of you.
Look, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is going into the Jordan ahead of you.
Now select twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one man from each tribe.

When the feet of the priests carrying the ark of God, the Lord of all the earth, come to rest in the Jordan, the river's flow will be cut off. The water coming from upstream will pile up in one place.”
The people left their tents to cross the Jordan, with the priests carrying the ark of the covenant out in front.
The Jordan floods its banks throughout harvest season. When the priests carrying the ark reached the river and their feet touched the water at the edge,

the water coming from upstream stopped and backed up far away at Adam, the town near Zarethan. The flow down to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, was cut off completely. So the people crossed near Jericho.
The priests carrying the ark of the LORD's covenant stood firmly on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan. All Israel crossed on dry ground until the whole nation was across.
When the whole nation had finished crossing the Jordan, the LORD spoke to Joshua.
“Choose twelve men from the people, one from each tribe.
Tell them, ‘Take twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, right where the priests stood. Carry them across with you and set them down where you camp tonight.’”
Joshua called the twelve men he'd selected from the Israelites, one out of each tribe.
He said to them, “Go in front of the ark of the LORD your God into the middle of the Jordan. Each of you pick up a stone and put it on your shoulder, one for each tribe of Israel.
These stones will be a sign among you. In years to come your children will ask, ‘What do these stones mean to you?’

Tell them, ‘The waters of the Jordan were cut off in front of the ark of the LORD's covenant. When the ark crossed the Jordan, the river stopped flowing. These stones will be a memorial for the Israelites forever.’”

The Israelites did what Joshua told them. They picked up twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, one for each tribe of Israel, as the LORD had told Joshua. They carried them to their camp and set them down there.
Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, where the priests carrying the ark of the covenant had stood. They're still there today.

The priests who carried the ark stood in the middle of the Jordan until everything the LORD had told Joshua to say to the people was done, just as Moses had instructed Joshua. The people hurried across.
Once everyone was across, the priests carried the LORD's ark across while the people watched.
The tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh crossed armed ahead of the other Israelites, just as Moses had told them.
About forty thousand men, armed and ready for war, crossed over before the LORD to the plains of Jericho for battle.
That day the LORD honored Joshua in front of all Israel. They held him in awe for the rest of his life, just as they had Moses.
The LORD spoke to Joshua.
“Tell the priests carrying the ark of the covenant to come up out of the Jordan.”
So Joshua told the priests, “Come up out of the Jordan!”

The priests carrying the ark of the LORD's covenant came up out of the middle of the Jordan. As soon as the soles of their feet came up onto dry ground, the Jordan flowed again and flooded its banks as before.
The people came up from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camped at Gilgal, on the eastern edge of Jericho.
Joshua set up the twelve stones they had taken from the Jordan in Gilgal.
He told the Israelites, “One day your children will ask their fathers, ‘What do these stones mean?’
Tell your children, ‘Israel crossed this Jordan on dry ground.
The LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan in front of you until you crossed, just as he dried up the Red Sea in front of us until we crossed.
He did it so every people on earth would know how mighty the LORD's hand is, and so you would honor the LORD your God forever.’”

The Amorite kings west of the Jordan and the Canaanite kings along the coast heard how the LORD had dried up the Jordan in front of the Israelites until we crossed. They lost heart, and there was no courage left in them to face Israel.
At that time the LORD told Joshua, “Make flint knives and circumcise the Israelite men again. This will be the second time.”
Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the Israelite men at the Hill of the Foreskins.
Here's why Joshua circumcised them. The men of fighting age who came out of Egypt had all died along the way in the wilderness after leaving Egypt.
All those who came out had been circumcised, but those born in the wilderness on the journey from Egypt hadn't been circumcised.

The Israelites traveled through the wilderness for forty years until all the fighting men who had come out of Egypt died, because they hadn't listened to the LORD. He swore they wouldn't see the land he had sworn to give our ancestors, a land flowing with milk and honey.
The LORD raised up their children in their place. Joshua circumcised them, because they hadn't been circumcised along the way.
When the whole nation had finished with the circumcision, everyone stayed where they were in camp until they healed.
The LORD told Joshua, “Today I've rolled away the shame of Egypt from you.” That's why the place is still called Gilgal today.
The Israelites camped at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho. There they kept the Passover on the evening of the fourteenth day of the month.
The very next day after Passover they ate food grown in the land: flatbread made without yeast and roasted grain.
The day after they ate the land's produce, the manna stopped. The Israelites didn't get manna anymore. That year they ate food from the land of Canaan.
When Joshua was near Jericho he looked up and saw a man standing in front of him with a drawn sword. Joshua walked over and asked him, “Are you on our side or our enemies' side?”
“Neither,” he said. “I've come as commander of the LORD's army.” Joshua fell facedown, bowed in worship, and asked, “What does my lord have to say to his servant?”
The commander of the LORD's army told Joshua, “Take off your sandals. The place you're standing on is holy.” So Joshua took them off.
Jericho was locked down tight because of the Israelites. Nobody went out or came in.
The LORD told Joshua, “Look, I've handed Jericho over to you, along with its king and its best fighters.
All your fighting men are to march around the city once a day for six days.
Seven priests will carry seven ram's-horn trumpets ahead of the ark. On the seventh day you'll march around the city seven times, and the priests will blow the trumpets.
When you hear one long blast from the ram's horn, everyone must shout as loudly as they can. The city wall will collapse, and everyone can go straight in from where they're standing.”
Joshua son of Nun called the priests and said, “Pick up the ark of the covenant, and have seven priests carry seven ram's-horn trumpets ahead of the LORD's ark.”
They told the people, “Move out! March around the city, with the armed men going ahead of the LORD's ark.”
After Joshua spoke, the seven priests went ahead of the LORD, blowing their seven ram's-horn trumpets, and the ark of the LORD's covenant went behind them.
The armed men went ahead of the priests blowing the trumpets, and the rear guard followed the ark. The trumpets kept sounding as they went.
Joshua told the people, “Don't shout, don't raise your voice, and don't say a word until the day I tell you to shout. Then shout.”
So Joshua had the LORD's ark carried once around the city. Then everyone went back to camp and stayed there.
Joshua got up early the next morning, and the priests picked up the LORD's ark.

The seven priests carrying the seven ram's horns went ahead of the LORD's ark and kept blowing the trumpets as they marched. The armed men went ahead of them, and the rear guard followed the LORD's ark. The horns kept sounding as they went.
On the second day they went around the city once, then went back to camp. They did this for six days.
On the seventh day they got up at dawn and marched around the city the same way, but seven times. That was the only day they went around seven times.
On the seventh trip around, the priests blew the trumpets and Joshua told the people, “Shout! The LORD has given you the city!
The city and everything in it are set apart for the LORD. Only Rahab the sex worker and those with her in her house will live, because she hid the messengers we sent.
Stay away from anything set apart for destruction. If you take any of it for yourselves after setting it apart, you'll bring a curse and trouble on Israel's camp.
All the silver, gold, and objects made of bronze and iron are holy to the LORD. They go into the LORD's treasury.”
The priests blew the trumpets, and when the people heard the blast, they let out a mighty shout. The wall collapsed, everyone went straight into the city from where they stood, and they took it.
They put everything in the city to the sword, men and women, young and old, cattle, sheep, and donkeys.
Joshua told the two men who had scouted the land, “Go into the woman's house and bring her and everyone who belongs to her out, as you swore to her.”
The two young scouts went in and brought Rahab out with her father, mother, brothers, and everyone who belonged to her. They brought out all her relatives and settled them outside Israel's camp.
They burned the city and everything in it. They put the silver, gold, and objects of bronze and iron in the treasury of the LORD's house.
Joshua spared Rahab the sex worker, her father's household, and everyone with her. She lives among the Israelites to this day because she hid the messengers Joshua sent to scout Jericho.

Then Joshua made the people take an oath: “Anyone who sets out to rebuild Jericho is cursed before the LORD. Laying its foundation will cost him his firstborn. Setting up its gates will cost him his youngest son.”
The LORD was with Joshua, and word about him spread across the entire land.

The Israelites broke faith over what had been set apart for the LORD. Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, from the tribe of Judah, took some of it. So the LORD's anger burned against the Israelites.
Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, near Beth Aven, east of Bethel. He told them to go up and scout the land, so they went and looked over Ai.
They came back and told Joshua, “You don't need to send everybody up. Two or three thousand men can attack Ai. There's no need to wear everyone out when there are so few people there.”
About three thousand men went up, but they ran from the men of Ai.
The men of Ai killed about thirty-six of them. They chased them from the city gate as far as Shebarim and struck them down on the slope. The people's courage melted like water.
Joshua tore his clothes and fell facedown before the LORD's ark. He and the elders of Israel stayed there until evening and put dust on their heads.

Joshua said, “Oh, Lord GOD, why did you bring these people across the Jordan at all, just to hand us over to the Amorites to be wiped out? If only we'd been content to stay on the other side of the Jordan!
Lord, what can I say now that Israel has turned and run from its enemies?
The Canaanites and everyone else in the land will hear about this, surround us, and erase our name from the earth. Then what will you do for your great name?”
The LORD told Joshua, “Get up! Why are you lying there facedown?
Israel has sinned. They broke the covenant I commanded them to keep. They took things that had been set apart. They stole, they lied, and they even hid those things among their own belongings.

That's why the Israelites can't stand against their enemies. They turn and run because they themselves are now set apart for destruction. I won't be with you anymore unless you destroy what was set apart and is still among you.

Get up and set the people apart. Tell them, ‘Get yourselves ready for tomorrow. The LORD, the God of Israel, says, “Israel, something set apart for destruction is among you. You cannot stand against your enemies until you remove it.”

In the morning come forward by tribe. The tribe the LORD singles out must come forward by clan. The clan he singles out must come forward by household. The household he singles out must come forward man by man.
Whoever is caught with what was set apart will be burned with everything he has, because he broke the LORD's covenant and did something disgraceful in Israel.’”
Joshua got up early the next morning and called Israel forward by tribe. The tribe of Judah was singled out.
He called Judah's clans forward, and the clan of Zerah was singled out. He called that clan forward man by man, and Zabdi was singled out.
He called Zabdi's household forward man by man, and Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was singled out.
Joshua told Achan, “My son, give glory to the LORD, the God of Israel, and confess to him. Tell me what you did. Don't hide it from me.”
Achan answered, “I really did sin against the LORD, the God of Israel. Here's what I did.

I saw a beautiful Babylonian robe among the plunder, along with two hundred shekels of silver and a wedge of gold weighing fifty shekels. I wanted them, so I took them. They're buried in the ground in the middle of my tent, with the silver underneath.”
Joshua sent messengers who ran to the tent. Sure enough, the objects were hidden there with the silver underneath.
They took everything from the middle of the tent and brought it to Joshua and all the Israelites. They laid it out before the LORD.

Joshua and all Israel took Achan, a descendant of Zerah, and the silver, the robe, the wedge of gold, his sons, his daughters, his cattle, donkeys, sheep, tent, and everything he had to the Valley of Achor.
Joshua said, “Why have you brought trouble on us? Today the LORD will bring trouble on you.” All Israel stoned him. They burned them and threw stones on them.
They piled up a great heap of stones over Achan, and it's still there today. The LORD turned away from his fierce anger. That's why that place is still called the Valley of Achor.
The LORD told Joshua, “Don't be afraid or lose heart. Get up and take all the fighting men with you to Ai. I've handed over its king, its people, its city, and its land to you.
Treat Ai and its king as you treated Jericho and its king, except this time you can keep the goods and livestock for yourselves. Set an ambush behind the city.”
Joshua and all the fighting men got ready to go up to Ai. Joshua chose thirty thousand of his best fighters and sent them out at night.
He told them, “Wait in ambush behind the city. Stay close and be ready.
I'll approach the city with everyone who's with me. When they come out against us like they did the first time, we'll run from them.
They'll come after us until we've drawn them away from the city. They'll think, ‘They're running away from us just like last time.’ So we'll keep running.
Then come out of hiding and take the city. The LORD your God will hand it over to you.
Once you've taken the city, burn it. Do what the LORD has said. Those are your orders.”
Joshua sent them out, and they took up their position between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai. Joshua spent that night with the people.
Joshua got up early, gathered the people, and went up to Ai with the elders of Israel at the head of the people.
All the fighting men with him marched up close to the city and camped to its north. A valley lay between them and Ai.
Joshua positioned about five thousand men in ambush between Bethel and Ai, west of the city.
With the main army north of the city and the men in ambush to its west, Joshua went into the middle of the valley that night.

When the king of Ai saw what was happening, he and his people got up early and hurried out to fight Israel at the appointed time in front of the Arabah. He had no idea men were waiting behind his city.
Joshua and all Israel pretended they'd been beaten and ran toward the wilderness.
Everyone in the city was called out to chase them. As they went after Joshua, they were drawn away from the city.
Every man in Ai and Bethel went after Israel. They left the city wide open and kept chasing.
The LORD told Joshua, “Hold out the javelin in your hand toward Ai. I'll hand the city over to you.” Joshua held his javelin out toward the city.
As soon as he stretched out his hand, the men in ambush rushed out of hiding, ran into the city, and took it. They quickly set it on fire.
The men of Ai looked back and saw smoke rising from the city into the sky. They had no way to escape in any direction. The Israelites who'd fled toward the wilderness turned on them.
When Joshua and all Israel saw that their men had taken the city and that smoke was rising, they turned back and struck down the men of Ai.
The other men came out of the city against them, leaving the men of Ai trapped between Israelites on both sides. Israel struck them down, leaving no survivors and letting no one escape.
They captured the king of Ai alive and brought him to Joshua.
Israel finished killing the people of Ai who had chased them into the open country of the wilderness. When they'd all fallen by the sword, Israel went back to Ai and put the city to the sword.
Twelve thousand men and women fell that day, the entire population of Ai.
Joshua kept his javelin stretched out until all the people of Ai had been destroyed.
Israel kept only the livestock and goods from the city, just as the LORD had commanded Joshua.
Joshua burned Ai and turned it into a desolate heap of ruins that remains to this day.

He hung the king of Ai on a tree until evening. At sunset, Joshua ordered the body taken down and thrown at the entrance to the city gate. They piled stones over it, and that great heap is still there today.
Then Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal to the LORD, the God of Israel.

Moses, the LORD's servant, had commanded the Israelites to build it this way in his book of the law, using uncut stones untouched by an iron tool. They offered burnt offerings to the LORD on it and sacrificed peace offerings.
There, with the Israelites watching, Joshua wrote a copy of Moses' law on the stones.

All Israel stood on both sides of the ark in front of the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the LORD's covenant. Their elders, officers, judges, native-born people, and foreigners were all there. Half stood in front of Mount Gerizim and half in front of Mount Ebal, as Moses, the LORD's servant, had originally commanded when he told them to bless the people of Israel.
Then Joshua read every word of the law, including the blessing and the curse, just as it was written in the book of the law.
Joshua read every word Moses had commanded before the whole gathering of Israel, including the women, the children, and the foreigners living among them.

All the kings across the Jordan heard what had happened. They were the kings of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, from the hill country, the lowlands, and all along the coast of the great sea toward Lebanon.
They united to fight against Joshua and Israel.
But when the people of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai,
they came up with a trick. They posed as ambassadors and loaded their donkeys with worn-out sacks and old wineskins that had split and been tied back together.
They put on old clothes and worn-out, patched sandals. All the bread they'd packed for the journey was dry and moldy.
They went to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal and told him and the Israelites, “We've come from far away. Make a treaty with us.”
The Israelites asked the Hivites, “What if you live right here among us? How could we make a treaty with you?”
They said to Joshua, “We're your servants.” Joshua asked, “Who are you, and where are you from?”
They answered, “Your servants have come from a very distant country because of the name of the LORD your God. We've heard about him and everything he did in Egypt.
We also heard what he did to both Amorite kings beyond the Jordan: King Sihon of Heshbon and King Og of Bashan, who ruled at Ashtaroth.
Our elders and everyone in our country told us, ‘Pack food for the trip and go meet them. Tell them, “We're your servants. Please make a treaty with us.”’
This bread was still hot when we packed it at home the day we left to come to you. Look at it now. It's dry and moldy.
These wineskins were new when we filled them, and look how torn they are now. Our clothes and sandals wore out because the trip was so long.”
The Israelites sampled their supplies without asking the LORD for guidance.
Joshua made peace with them and signed a treaty promising to let them live. The leaders of the community swore to keep it.
Three days after they made the treaty, the Israelites found out these people were their neighbors and lived right among them.
The Israelites set out and reached their towns on the third day. The towns were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath Jearim.
The Israelites didn't attack them, because the leaders of the community had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. The whole community complained against the leaders.
But the leaders told the whole community, “We've sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. We can't touch them now.
Here's what we'll do: we'll let them live, so God's anger won't come on us for breaking the oath we swore to them.”
The leaders said, “Let them live.” So the Gibeonites became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole community, just as the leaders said.
Joshua called them in and asked, “Why did you deceive us by saying, ‘We live far away,’ when you live right among us?
Now you're under a curse. Some of you will always serve as slaves, cutting wood and carrying water for the house of my God.”

They answered Joshua, “Your servants were told for certain that the LORD your God commanded his servant Moses to give you this whole land and destroy everyone living in it ahead of you. We were scared for our lives because of you. That's why we did it.
Now we're in your hands. Do whatever you think is good and right.”
Joshua did as he said. He rescued them from the Israelites, who otherwise would have killed them.
That day Joshua made them woodcutters and water carriers for the community and for the LORD's altar at the place the LORD would choose. They still do that work today.

Adoni-Zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard that Joshua had captured Ai and completely destroyed it. Joshua had done to Ai and its king what he had done to Jericho and its king. Adoni-Zedek also heard that the people of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were living among them.
That frightened them, because Gibeon was as large as one of the royal cities, bigger than Ai, and all its men were strong fighters.
So King Adoni-Zedek of Jerusalem sent word to King Hoham of Hebron, King Piram of Jarmuth, King Japhia of Lachish, and King Debir of Eglon.
“Come up and help me attack Gibeon. They've made peace with Joshua and the Israelites.”
The five Amorite kings, the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon, gathered with all their armies. They went up, camped outside Gibeon, and attacked it.

The men of Gibeon sent a message to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal. “Don't abandon your servants! Come quickly and save us! Help us! All the Amorite kings from the hill country have joined forces against us.”
Joshua went up from Gilgal with the whole army, including all his best fighters.
The LORD told Joshua, “Don't be afraid of them. I've handed them over to you. None of them will be able to stand against you.”
Joshua marched all night from Gilgal and caught them by surprise.
The LORD threw them into confusion before Israel and struck them down in great numbers at Gibeon. He chased them up the road toward Beth Horon and struck them down as far as Azekah and Makkedah.

As they fled from Israel down the slope at Beth Horon, the LORD hurled huge hailstones from the sky on them all the way to Azekah. More died from the hailstones than the Israelites killed with the sword.
On the day the LORD handed the Amorites over to Israel, Joshua spoke to the LORD in front of the Israelites. He said, “Sun, stand still over Gibeon! Moon, stop over the Valley of Aijalon!”

The sun stood still and the moon stopped until the nation had taken vengeance on its enemies. Isn't this written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stayed in the middle of the sky and didn't go down for about a whole day.
There had never been a day like it before, and there hasn't been one since, when the LORD listened to a human voice like that. The LORD fought for Israel.
Joshua and all Israel returned to their camp at Gilgal.
The five kings had run away and hidden in a cave at Makkedah.
Someone told Joshua, “We've found the five kings. They're hiding in the cave at Makkedah.”
Joshua said, “Roll large stones over the cave entrance and leave some men there to guard them.
The rest of you keep moving. Go after your enemies and strike them from behind. Keep them from getting into their towns, because the LORD your God has handed them over to you.”
Joshua and the Israelites struck down nearly all of them in a great slaughter. The few survivors got into the fortified towns.
Then all the people returned safely to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. No one spoke a word against any of the Israelites.
Joshua said, “Open the cave entrance and bring those five kings out to me.”
They brought the five kings out of the cave to him: the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon.

When the kings were brought out, Joshua called all the men of Israel and told the commanders who had gone with him, “Come forward and put your feet on these kings' necks.” They came forward and did it.
Joshua told them, “Don't be afraid or lose heart. Be strong and brave. This is what the LORD will do to every enemy you fight.”
Then Joshua struck the kings down, killed them, and hung them on five trees. They hung there until evening.
At sunset Joshua ordered them taken down. The men threw the bodies into the cave where the kings had hidden and covered its entrance with large stones that are still there today.

That same day Joshua captured Makkedah and put its people and king to the sword. He destroyed the city and everyone in it, leaving no survivors. He did to its king what he'd done to the king of Jericho.
Joshua and all Israel went from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against it.
The LORD handed Libnah and its king over to Israel too. Joshua put everyone in the town to the sword, leaving no survivors. He did to its king what he'd done to the king of Jericho.
Joshua and all Israel went from Libnah to Lachish, camped against it, and attacked it.
The LORD handed Lachish over to Israel. Joshua took it on the second day and put everyone in it to the sword, just as he'd done to Libnah.
Then King Horam of Gezer came to help Lachish. Joshua struck him and his people down until none were left.
Joshua and all Israel went from Lachish to Eglon, camped against it, and attacked it.
They captured it that day and put its people to the sword. Joshua destroyed everyone in the city that day, just as he'd done at Lachish.
Joshua and all Israel went up from Eglon to Hebron and attacked it.
They took Hebron and put its king, everyone living there, and the people of its surrounding towns to the sword. As at Eglon, Joshua destroyed the town and everyone in it, leaving no survivors.
Then Joshua turned back with all Israel to Debir and fought against it.

They captured Debir, its king, and its towns. They put them all to the sword and destroyed everyone, leaving no survivors. Joshua did to Debir and its king what he'd done to Hebron and to Libnah and its king.

Joshua defeated the whole region: the hill country, the south, the lowlands, the slopes, and all their kings. He left no survivors and destroyed everything that breathed, as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded.
Joshua defeated them from Kadesh Barnea to Gaza and throughout the whole region of Goshen as far as Gibeon.
Joshua captured all these kings and their lands in one campaign because the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel.
Then Joshua and all Israel returned to their camp at Gilgal.
When King Jabin of Hazor heard what had happened, he sent word to King Jobab of Madon and to the kings of Shimron and Achshaph.
He also sent word to the kings to the north in the hill country, in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, in the lowlands, and in the heights of Dor to the west.
He contacted the Canaanites in the east and west, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites below Mount Hermon in the land of Mizpah.
They came out with all their armies. There were as many people as grains of sand on the seashore, along with a huge number of horses and chariots.
All these kings joined forces and camped together by the waters of Merom to fight Israel.
The LORD told Joshua, “Don't be afraid of them. By this time tomorrow I'll hand them all over to Israel, slain. You'll hamstring their horses and burn their chariots.”
Joshua and all his fighting men surprised them by the waters of Merom and attacked.

The LORD handed them over to Israel. The Israelites struck them down and chased them as far as Great Sidon, Misrephoth Maim, and east to the Valley of Mizpah. They kept striking until there were no survivors.
Joshua did what the LORD had told him. He hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots.
Joshua then turned back, captured Hazor, and killed its king with the sword. Hazor had once been the most powerful of all those kingdoms.
They put everyone in Hazor to the sword and destroyed them completely. No one was left alive. Joshua burned the city.
Joshua captured the towns of all those kings along with the kings themselves. He put them to the sword and destroyed them completely, just as Moses, the LORD's servant, had commanded.
Israel left the towns that stood on their raised mounds unburned, apart from Hazor, which Joshua burned.
The Israelites kept all the goods and livestock from those towns as plunder. They put every person to the sword until no one was left alive.
The LORD had given these commands to his servant Moses, and Moses passed them on to Joshua. Joshua carried them out and left nothing undone that the LORD had commanded Moses.
Joshua took that whole region: the hill country, the entire south, all of Goshen, the lowlands, the Arabah, and the hill country of Israel with its lowlands.
The territory stretched from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, to Baal Gad in the Lebanon Valley below Mount Hermon. Joshua captured all their kings, struck them down, and killed them.
Joshua fought against those kings for a long time.
Only the Hivites in Gibeon made peace with the Israelites. Israel took every other city in battle.
The LORD hardened their hearts so they'd come out to fight Israel, so that they'd be completely destroyed and shown no mercy, as the LORD had commanded Moses.
At that time Joshua cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, Debir, and Anab, and from all the hills of Judah and Israel. He completely destroyed them and their towns.
None of the Anakim were left in Israelite territory. Some remained only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod.
Joshua took the whole land just as the LORD had told Moses. He divided it among Israel's tribes as their inheritance. Then the land had rest from war.
These are the kings the Israelites defeated east of the Jordan. Israel took their land from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, including the whole eastern Arabah.

King Sihon of the Amorites lived in Heshbon. He ruled from Aroer on the edge of the Arnon Valley, including the middle of the valley and half of Gilead, as far as the Jabbok River on the Ammonite border.
He also ruled the eastern Arabah from the Sea of Chinneroth to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, on the way to Beth Jeshimoth, and south below the slopes of Pisgah.
The Israelites also took the territory of King Og of Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim, who lived in Ashtaroth and Edrei.
He ruled Mount Hermon, Salecah, and all of Bashan as far as the borders of the Geshurites and Maacathites. He also ruled half of Gilead, up to the border of King Sihon of Heshbon.
Moses, the LORD's servant, and the Israelites defeated these kings. Moses gave their land to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh as their own.

Here are the kings Joshua and the Israelites defeated west of the Jordan, from Baal Gad in the Lebanon Valley to Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir. Joshua divided that land among Israel's tribes as their own.

The land included the hill country, the lowlands, the Arabah, the slopes, the wilderness, and the south. These were the lands of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
One king of Jericho and one king of Ai near Bethel.
One king of Jerusalem and one king of Hebron.
One king of Jarmuth and one king of Lachish.
One king of Eglon and one king of Gezer.
One king of Debir and one king of Geder.
One king of Hormah and one king of Arad.
One king of Libnah and one king of Adullam.
One king of Makkedah and one king of Bethel.
One king of Tappuah and one king of Hepher.
One king of Aphek and one king of Lassharon.
One king of Madon and one king of Hazor.
One king of Shimron Meron and one king of Achshaph.
One king of Taanach and one king of Megiddo.
One king of Kedesh and one king of Jokneam in Carmel.
One king of Dor in the heights of Dor and one king of Goiim in Gilgal.
One king of Tirzah. That makes thirty-one kings in all.
Joshua was getting very old. The LORD told him, “You're well along in years, and there's still a lot of land to take possession of.
Here's the land that remains: all the territory of the Philistines and all the territory of the Geshurites,

from the Shihor near Egypt north to the border of Ekron, which is counted as Canaanite territory. It includes the territory of the five Philistine rulers in Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, as well as the Avvim
in the south. There's also all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah, which belongs to the Sidonians, as far as Aphek at the Amorite border.
There's the land of the Gebalites and all Lebanon toward the east, from Baal Gad below Mount Hermon to the entrance of Hamath.

I'll drive out the people of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth Maim, including all the Sidonians, ahead of the Israelites. Your job is to assign the land to Israel as an inheritance, just as I told you.
Now divide this land as an inheritance among the nine tribes and the half tribe of Manasseh.”
The other half of Manasseh received its inheritance alongside Reuben and Gad on the east side of the Jordan, just as Moses, the LORD's servant, had assigned it.
It stretched from Aroer on the edge of the Arnon Valley and the town in the middle of the valley, across the whole plain of Medeba as far as Dibon.
It included all the towns of King Sihon of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon, as far as the Ammonite border.
It included Gilead, the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, all of Mount Hermon, and all of Bashan as far as Salecah.
It also included the entire kingdom of Og in Bashan, who ruled in Ashtaroth and Edrei and was one of the last of the Rephaim. Moses defeated those kings and drove them out.
The Israelites didn't drive out the Geshurites or Maacathites, so the people of Geshur and Maacath still live among Israel today.
Levi was the only tribe that got no land as an inheritance. Their inheritance was the offerings made by fire to the LORD, the God of Israel, just as he had promised them.
Moses gave land to the tribe of Reuben, clan by clan.
Their territory ran from Aroer on the edge of the Arnon Valley, taking in the town in the middle of the valley and the whole plain near Medeba.
It included Heshbon and all its towns on the plain: Dibon, Bamoth Baal, and Beth Baal Meon,
along with Jahaz, Kedemoth, and Mephaath,
Kiriathaim, Sibmah, and Zereth Shahar on the hill in the valley,
Beth Peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth Jeshimoth.

It included all the towns on the plain and the entire kingdom of Sihon, the Amorite king who ruled in Heshbon. Moses defeated him and the Midianite chiefs Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, who were rulers under Sihon and lived in the land.
The Israelites also put Balaam son of Beor, the diviner, to the sword along with the others they killed.
The bank of the Jordan marked Reuben's border. These towns and their villages were the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben, clan by clan.
Moses also gave land to the tribe of Gad, clan by clan.
Their territory included Jazer, all the towns of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites as far as Aroer near Rabbah.
It stretched from Heshbon to Ramath Mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the border of Debir.

In the valley it included Beth Haram, Beth Nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of King Sihon's kingdom in Heshbon. It ran along the east bank of the Jordan as far as the far end of the Sea of Chinnereth.
These towns and their villages were the inheritance of the tribe of Gad, clan by clan.
Moses gave an inheritance to half the tribe of Manasseh, assigning it to their clans.
Their territory stretched from Mahanaim and included all Bashan, the entire kingdom of King Og of Bashan, and all sixty of Jair's settlements in Bashan.
Half of Gilead, along with Ashtaroth and Edrei, the cities of Og's kingdom in Bashan, went to the descendants of Machir son of Manasseh. It was given to half of Machir's descendants, clan by clan.
These are the inheritances Moses assigned on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan across from Jericho.
Moses gave no land as an inheritance to the tribe of Levi. The LORD, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, just as he told them.
These are the lands the Israelites received as their inheritance in Canaan. Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the family leaders of Israel's tribes assigned them their shares.
The nine tribes and the half tribe received their shares by lot, just as the LORD had commanded through Moses.
Moses had already given the other two and a half tribes their inheritance across the Jordan. The Levites received no land among them as an inheritance.
Joseph's descendants made up two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. The Levites received only towns to live in, with pasture around them for their livestock and space for their property.
The Israelites divided up the land the way the LORD had told Moses.
The people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said, “You know what the LORD told Moses, the man of God, about you and me at Kadesh Barnea.
I was forty years old when Moses, the LORD's servant, sent me from Kadesh Barnea to scout the land. I came back and told him honestly what I thought.
The men who went with me made the people lose heart, but I followed the LORD my God with my whole heart.
That day Moses swore, ‘The land you walked on will belong to you and your children forever as an inheritance, because you followed the LORD my God with your whole heart.’
The LORD has kept me alive these forty-five years, just as he promised, since he told Moses this while Israel was traveling in the wilderness. Here I am today, eighty-five years old.
I'm still as strong today as I was when Moses sent me out. I have the same strength now as I did then, for battle and for going out and coming in.
So give me this hill country the LORD spoke about that day. You heard then that the Anakim lived there in large, fortified towns. If the LORD is with me, I'll drive them out, just as he said.”
Joshua blessed Caleb son of Jephunneh and gave him Hebron as his inheritance.
Hebron still belongs to Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite as his inheritance because he followed the LORD, the God of Israel, with his whole heart.
Hebron used to be called Kiriath Arba, after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim. Then the land had rest from war.
The land assigned by lot to Judah, clan by clan, stretched south to Edom's border and the wilderness of Zin, at the far southern end.
Their southern border began at the southern end of the Salt Sea, at the bay facing south.
It ran south of the Akrabbim Pass, went through Zin, and climbed south of Kadesh Barnea. It went past Hezron, up to Addar, and turned toward Karka.
It continued to Azmon, reached the Brook of Egypt, and ended at the sea. That's your southern border.
The eastern border followed the Salt Sea as far as the mouth of the Jordan. The northern border started at the bay where the Jordan enters the sea.
From there it went up to Beth Hoglah, passed north of Beth Arabah, and climbed to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben.

The border climbed from the Valley of Achor to Debir and turned north toward Gilgal, opposite the Adummim Pass on the south side of the stream. It ran past the waters of En Shemesh and ended at En Rogel.

It climbed through the Valley of Ben Hinnom, along the south side of the Jebusite city, also called Jerusalem. Then it climbed to the hilltop west of the Hinnom Valley, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim.
From that hilltop the border ran to the spring at Nephtoah, then to the towns of Mount Ephron, and on to Baalah, also called Kiriath Jearim.
From Baalah it turned west to Mount Seir, passed along the north side of Mount Jearim, also called Chesalon, came down to Beth Shemesh, and went past Timnah.
The border ran along the north side of Ekron, went on to Shikkeron, passed Mount Baalah, and reached Jabneel before ending at the sea.
The coastline of the great sea marked the western border. These were the boundaries of Judah's land, clan by clan.
As the LORD had commanded him, Joshua gave Caleb son of Jephunneh a share among the people of Judah. He gave him Kiriath Arba, also called Hebron, which had been named for Arba, the father of Anak.
Caleb drove out three descendants of Anak: Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.
Then Caleb went up against the people of Debir, which used to be called Kiriath Sepher.
Caleb said, “I'll give my daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever attacks Kiriath Sepher and captures it.”
Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's brother, captured the town, so Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah in marriage.
When Achsah came to Othniel, she urged him to ask her father for a field. She got down from her donkey, and Caleb asked her, “What would you like?”
She said, “Give me a blessing. You've given me land in the south, so please give me springs of water too.” Caleb gave her the upper and lower springs.
This was the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, clan by clan.
Judah's towns farthest south toward Edom's border were Kabzeel, Eder, and Jagur,
Kinah, Dimonah, and Adadah,
Kedesh, Hazor, and Ithnan,
Ziph, Telem, and Bealoth,
Hazor Hadattah and Kerioth Hezron, also called Hazor,
Amam, Shema, and Moladah,
Hazar Gaddah, Heshmon, and Beth Pelet,
Hazar Shual, Beersheba, and Biziothiah,
Baalah, Iim, and Ezem,
Eltolad, Chesil, and Hormah,
Ziklag, Madmannah, and Sansannah,
Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon. There were twenty-nine towns in all, with their villages.
In the lowlands were Eshtaol, Zorah, and Ashnah,
Zanoah, En Gannim, Tappuah, and Enam,
Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, and Azekah,
Shaaraim, Adithaim, and Gederah, also called Gederothaim. There were fourteen towns with their villages.
There were also Zenan, Hadashah, and Migdal Gad,
Dilean, Mizpah, and Joktheel,
Lachish, Bozkath, and Eglon,
Cabbon, Lahmam, and Chitlish,
Gederoth, Beth Dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah. There were sixteen towns with their villages.
There were also Libnah, Ether, and Ashan,
Iphtah, Ashnah, and Nezib,
Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah. There were nine towns with their villages.
Judah also received Ekron and its towns and villages,
and everything from Ekron to the sea near Ashdod, including the villages.
Judah received Ashdod and its towns and villages, and Gaza and its towns and villages, as far as the Brook of Egypt and the coastline of the great sea.
In the hill country were Shamir, Jattir, and Socoh,
Dannah and Kiriath Sannah, also called Debir,
Anab, Eshtemoh, and Anim,
Goshen, Holon, and Giloh. There were eleven towns with their villages.
There were also Arab, Dumah, and Eshan,
Janim, Beth Tappuah, and Aphekah,
Humtah, Kiriath Arba, also called Hebron, and Zior. There were nine towns with their villages.
There were also Maon, Carmel, Ziph, and Jutah,
Jezreel, Jokdeam, and Zanoah,
Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah. There were ten towns with their villages.
There were also Halhul, Beth Zur, and Gedor,
Maarath, Beth Anoth, and Eltekon. There were six towns with their villages.
There were also Kiriath Baal, known as Kiriath Jearim, and Rabbah. There were two towns with their villages.
In the wilderness were Beth Arabah, Middin, and Secacah,
Nibshan, the City of Salt, and En Gedi. There were six towns with their villages.
The people of Judah couldn't drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, so the Jebusites still live there alongside the people of Judah today.
The land assigned by lot to Joseph's descendants began at the Jordan near Jericho, east of the springs of Jericho. It went up through the wilderness from Jericho into the hill country toward Bethel.
It ran from Bethel to Luz and continued along the border of the Archites to Ataroth.
Then it went down west to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as Lower Beth Horon and Gezer, and ended at the sea.
Joseph's descendants, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.
This was Ephraim's territory, clan by clan. On the east, the boundary of their inheritance ran from Ataroth Addar to Upper Beth Horon.
The border ran west, with Michmethath to the north. Then it turned east toward Taanath Shiloh and passed east of Janoah.
It went down from Janoah to Ataroth and Naarah, reached Jericho, and ended at the Jordan.
From Tappuah the border ran west along the Kanah Brook and ended at the sea. This was Ephraim's inheritance, clan by clan.
They also received towns set apart for them within Manasseh's inheritance, including all the villages belonging to those towns.
They didn't drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer. Those Canaanites still live within Ephraim's territory today and have been made to do forced labor.
This was the land assigned by lot to the tribe of Manasseh, Joseph's firstborn. Machir, Manasseh's firstborn and the father of Gilead, received Gilead and Bashan because he was a warrior.
Land also went to the rest of Manasseh's descendants, clan by clan: Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These were the clans descended from the sons of Manasseh son of Joseph.
Zelophehad son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had daughters but no sons. His daughters were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.

They came before Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders. They said, “The LORD told Moses to give us an inheritance alongside our brothers.” So Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father's brothers, just as the LORD had commanded.
Manasseh received ten shares in addition to Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan.
That's because Manasseh's daughters received an inheritance alongside his sons. The rest of Manasseh's sons received Gilead.
Manasseh's border ran from Asher to Michmethath, near Shechem. From there it turned to the right toward the people of En Tappuah.
The land around Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah on Manasseh's border belonged to Ephraim.
The border went down to the Kanah Brook. On the south side of the brook were Ephraim's towns among the towns of Manasseh. Manasseh's border ran along the north side of the brook and ended at the sea.
The land to the south belonged to Ephraim and the land to the north to Manasseh, with the sea marking Manasseh's boundary. Manasseh's territory reached Asher on the north and Issachar on the east.
Within Issachar and Asher, Manasseh received Beth Shean and Ibleam with their towns, and the people of Dor, Endor, Taanach, and Megiddo with their towns. This included three hill districts.
The people of Manasseh couldn't drive out the people of those towns. The Canaanites were determined to stay in that land.
When the Israelites grew stronger, they made the Canaanites do forced labor, but they never drove them out completely.
Joseph's descendants asked Joshua, “Why have you given us only one allotment, one share of land? There are so many of us because the LORD has blessed us all this time.”
Joshua said, “If there are so many of you and Ephraim's hill country is too small, go into the forest in the territory of the Perizzites and Rephaim and clear land there for yourselves.”

Joseph's descendants said, “The hill country isn't enough for us. And all the Canaanites in the valley have iron chariots, both the ones in Beth Shean and its towns and the ones in the Valley of Jezreel.”
Joshua told the house of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, “There are many of you, and you're strong. You'll have more than one share.
The hill country will be yours. It's forest now, but you'll clear it, and it'll be yours to its farthest edge. You'll drive the Canaanites out, even though they have iron chariots and are strong.”
The whole community of Israel gathered at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting there. The land was now under their control.
Seven tribes of Israel still hadn't received their shares of the land.
Joshua asked the Israelites, “How long are you going to put off taking possession of the land the LORD, the God of your ancestors, has given you?
Choose three men from each tribe. I'll send them to walk through the land and write down how it can be divided for your inheritance. Then they'll come back to me.
They're to divide it into seven shares. Judah will stay in its territory to the south, and Joseph's descendants in theirs to the north.
Survey the land in seven sections and bring the description back to me. I'll cast lots for you here before the LORD our God.

The Levites won't get a share among you because serving as the LORD's priests is their inheritance. Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh already received their inheritance east of the Jordan from Moses, the LORD's servant.”
As the men set out, Joshua told the surveyors, “Walk through the land, write down what you find, and come back to me. I'll cast lots for you here at Shiloh in the LORD's presence.”
The men went through the land and wrote down a survey, listing the towns in seven sections. Then they came back to Joshua at the camp in Shiloh.
Joshua cast lots for them before the LORD at Shiloh. There he divided the land among the Israelites according to their groups.
The lot came up for the tribe of Benjamin, clan by clan. Their territory lay between Judah's land and that of Joseph's descendants.
Their northern border started at the Jordan, went up along the north side of Jericho, and climbed west through the hill country. It ended at the wilderness of Beth Aven.
From there it ran to the south side of Luz, also called Bethel. Then it went down to Ataroth Addar near the hill south of Lower Beth Horon.
From the hill south of Beth Horon, the border turned south on the west side and ended at Kiriath Baal, also called Kiriath Jearim, a town of Judah. That was the western border.
The southern border began at the edge of Kiriath Jearim, ran west, and reached the spring at Nephtoah.

From there it went down to the foot of the hill opposite the Valley of Ben Hinnom, at the north end of the Valley of Rephaim. It went down through the Hinnom Valley along the south side of the Jebusite city, then down to En Rogel.
The border turned north to En Shemesh and reached Geliloth opposite the Adummim Pass. Then it went down to the Stone of Bohan son of Reuben.
It continued along the north side of the slope facing the Arabah and went down into the Arabah.
It passed north of Beth Hoglah and ended at the northern bay of the Salt Sea, at the southern end of the Jordan. That was the southern border.
The Jordan marked the eastern border. Those were the boundaries of Benjamin's inheritance, clan by clan.
The towns belonging to Benjamin's clans were Jericho, Beth Hoglah, and Emek Keziz,
Beth Arabah, Zemaraim, and Bethel,
Avvim, Parah, and Ophrah,
Chephar Ammoni, Ophni, and Geba. There were twelve towns and their villages.
There were also Gibeon, Ramah, and Beeroth,
Mizpeh, Chephirah, and Mozah,
Rekem, Irpeel, and Taralah,
Zelah, Eleph, the Jebusite city also called Jerusalem, Gibeath, and Kiriath. There were fourteen towns and their villages. This was Benjamin's inheritance, clan by clan.
The second lot came up for Simeon, clan by clan. Their inheritance lay within Judah's territory.
They received Beersheba, also called Sheba, and Moladah,
Hazar Shual, Balah, and Ezem,
Eltolad, Bethul, and Hormah,
Ziklag, Beth Marcaboth, and Hazar Susah,
Beth Lebaoth and Sharuhen. There were thirteen towns with their villages.
They also received Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan, four towns with their villages,
and all the villages around these towns as far as Baalath Beer, also called Ramah of the South. This was the inheritance of Simeon's tribe, clan by clan.
Simeon received its inheritance from Judah's share because Judah's territory was more than it needed. That's why Simeon's inheritance lay within Judah's land.
The third lot came up for Zebulun, clan by clan. The border of their inheritance reached Sarid.
From there it climbed west to Maralah, reached Dabbesheth, and went to the stream across from Jokneam.
From Sarid it turned east toward the border of Chisloth Tabor, went on to Daberath, and climbed to Japhia.
It kept going east to Gath Hepher and Ethkazin, then reached Rimmon, which stretches toward Neah.
The border curved north toward Hannathon and ended at the Valley of Iphtah El.
The territory included Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem. There were twelve towns with their villages.
These towns and villages were the inheritance of Zebulun's descendants, clan by clan.
The fourth lot came up for Issachar, clan by clan.
Their territory included Jezreel, Chesulloth, and Shunem,
Hapharaim, Shion, and Anaharath,
Rabbith, Kishion, and Ebez,
Remeth, Engannim, En Haddah, and Beth Pazzez.
The boundary reached Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth Shemesh and ended at the Jordan. There were sixteen towns with their villages.
These towns and villages were the inheritance of Issachar's tribe, clan by clan.
The fifth lot came up for Asher's tribe, clan by clan.
Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, and Achshaph,
Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. Its border reached west to Carmel and Shihorlibnath.
The border turned east to Beth Dagon and touched Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtah El. From there it headed north to Beth Emek and Neiel, and went out to Cabul on the left.
It included Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, and Kanah, and went as far as Great Sidon.
The border turned toward Ramah and the fortified city of Tyre, then turned again toward Hosah. It ended at the sea in the region of Achzib.
It also included Ummah, Aphek, and Rehob. There were twenty-two towns with their villages.
These towns and villages were the inheritance of Asher's tribe, clan by clan.
The sixth lot came up for Naphtali, clan by clan.
Their border ran from Heleph and the oak at Zaanannim, through Adami-nekeb and Jabneel to Lakkum, and ended at the Jordan.
The border turned west to Aznoth Tabor and went on to Hukkok. It reached Zebulun on the south, Asher on the west, and Judah at the Jordan on the east.
The fortified towns were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth,
Adamah, Ramah, and Hazor,
Kedesh, Edrei, and En Hazor,
Iron, Migdal El, Horem, Beth Anath, and Beth Shemesh. There were nineteen towns with their villages.
These towns and villages were the inheritance of Naphtali's tribe, clan by clan.
The seventh lot came up for Dan's tribe, clan by clan.
Their territory included Zorah, Eshtaol, and Irshemesh,
Shaalabbin, Aijalon, and Ithlah,
Elon, Timnah, and Ekron,
Eltekeh, Gibbethon, and Baalath,
Jehud, Bene Berak, and Gath Rimmon,
Me Jarkon, Rakkon, and the territory opposite Joppa.

Dan's territory extended beyond those boundaries. The people of Dan went up and fought against Leshem, captured it, and put its people to the sword. They took possession of it, settled there, and renamed it Dan after their ancestor.
These towns and villages were the inheritance of Dan's tribe, clan by clan.
When the Israelites finished assigning the land by its boundaries, they gave Joshua son of Nun an inheritance among them.
As the LORD had commanded, they gave him the town he asked for, Timnathserah in the hill country of Ephraim. He built up the town and lived there.

These were the inheritances Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the Israelite tribes assigned by lot at Shiloh, before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. That finished the division of the land.
The LORD spoke to Joshua.
“Tell the Israelites, ‘Set aside the cities of refuge I told you about through Moses.
Anyone who kills someone by accident can run to one of these cities for safety from the relative seeking to avenge the death.

The person must flee to one of these cities, stand at the entrance to the city gate, and explain what happened to the city elders. The elders must take the person into the city and give them a place to live among them.
If the avenger of blood comes after that person, the elders must refuse to hand them over. The killing was unintentional, and the person had no prior hatred for the neighbor who died.

The person must live in that city until they stand before the community for judgment and until the high priest serving at the time dies. Then they may go back to their own home, in the city they fled from.’”
They set aside Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath Arba, also called Hebron, in the hill country of Judah.
East of the Jordan across from Jericho, they set aside Bezer on the wilderness plain from the tribe of Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead from the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan from the tribe of Manasseh.

These were the cities designated for all Israelites and for foreigners living among them. Anyone who killed someone unintentionally could flee there and be safe from the avenger of blood until they stood trial before the community.
Then the heads of the Levite families approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the family leaders of Israel's tribes.
At Shiloh in Canaan they said, “The LORD commanded through Moses that we be given towns to live in and pasture for our livestock.”
So the Israelites took towns and their pasturelands from their own inheritance and gave them to the Levites as the LORD had commanded.
The lot came up for the Kohathite clans. Aaron the priest's descendants, who were Levites, received thirteen towns by lot from Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin.
The rest of Kohath's descendants received ten towns by lot from the clans of Ephraim, Dan, and half the tribe of Manasseh.
Gershon's descendants received thirteen towns by lot from the clans of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and half the tribe of Manasseh in Bashan.
Merari's descendants received twelve towns from Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun, clan by clan.
The Israelites gave these towns and their pasturelands to the Levites by lot, just as the LORD had commanded through Moses.
From the tribes of Judah and Simeon they gave the towns listed here by name.
These went to Aaron's descendants, part of the Kohathite clans of Levi, because the first lot was theirs.
They gave them Kiriath Arba, also called Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, with the pasturelands around it. The town was named after Arba, the father of Anak.
The fields and villages belonging to the town went to Caleb son of Jephunneh as his own property.
Aaron the priest's descendants received Hebron, a city of refuge for someone who had killed another person, and Libnah, both with their pasturelands.
They received Jattir and Eshtemoa, both with their pasturelands,
Holon and Debir, both with their pasturelands,
and Ain, Juttah, and Beth Shemesh with their pasturelands. That made nine towns from those two tribes.
From Benjamin they received Gibeon and Geba, both with their pasturelands,
and Anathoth and Almon, both with their pasturelands. That made four towns.
Aaron's descendants, the priests, received thirteen towns in all, with their pasturelands.
The other Levite clans descended from Kohath received towns by lot from the tribe of Ephraim.
They received Shechem in Ephraim's hill country, a city of refuge for someone who had killed another person, and Gezer, both with their pasturelands.
They also received Kibzaim and Beth Horon, both with their pasturelands. That made four towns.
From Dan they received Elteke and Gibbethon, both with their pasturelands,
and Aijalon and Gath Rimmon, both with their pasturelands. That made four towns.
From half the tribe of Manasseh they received Taanach and Gath Rimmon, both with their pasturelands. That made two towns.
The other Kohathite clans received ten towns in all, with their pasturelands.

The Levite clans descended from Gershon received two towns from half the tribe of Manasseh: Golan in Bashan, a city of refuge for someone who had killed another person, and Be Eshterah, both with their pasturelands.
From Issachar they received Kishion and Daberath, both with their pasturelands,
and Jarmuth and En Gannim, both with their pasturelands. That made four towns.
From Asher they received Mishal and Abdon, both with their pasturelands,
and Helkath and Rehob, both with their pasturelands. That made four towns.
From Naphtali they received Kedesh in Galilee, a city of refuge for someone who had killed another person, and Hammothdor and Kartan, all with their pasturelands. That made three towns.
The Gershonite clans received thirteen towns in all, with their pasturelands.
The rest of the Levites, the clans descended from Merari, received Jokneam and Kartah from Zebulun, both with their pasturelands,
and Dimnah and Nahalal, both with their pasturelands. That made four towns.
From Reuben they received Bezer and Jahaz, both with their pasturelands,
and Kedemoth and Mephaath, both with their pasturelands. That made four towns.
From Gad they received Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge for someone who had killed another person, and Mahanaim, both with their pasturelands,
and Heshbon and Jazer, both with their pasturelands. That made four towns in all.
That was the share assigned by lot to the remaining Levite clans, the descendants of Merari: twelve towns, clan by clan.
The Levites received forty-eight towns with their pasturelands within the land the Israelites owned.
Each of these towns came with the pastureland around it. That was true of all the towns.
The LORD gave Israel all the land he'd sworn to give their ancestors. They took possession of it and settled there.
The LORD gave them rest on every side, just as he'd sworn to their ancestors. None of their enemies could stand against them. The LORD handed them all over to Israel.
Every good promise the LORD had made to the house of Israel came true. Every one of them.
Joshua called together the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh.
He told them, “You've done everything Moses, the LORD's servant, commanded you, and you've listened to me in everything I told you to do.
All this time you've stayed with your fellow Israelites and carried out the duty the LORD your God gave you.
Now the LORD your God has given your fellow Israelites rest, just as he promised. So go back to your tents and to the land Moses, the LORD's servant, gave you across the Jordan.

Be very careful to follow the command and the law Moses, the LORD's servant, gave you. Love the LORD your God, follow all his ways, keep his commands, hold on to him, and serve him with all your heart and all your soul.”
Joshua blessed them and sent them home to their tents.

Moses had given half the tribe of Manasseh an inheritance in Bashan. Joshua gave the other half land among their fellow Israelites west of the Jordan. As he sent the eastern tribes back to their tents, he blessed them.
He told them, “Go home with all this wealth: plenty of livestock, silver, gold, bronze, iron, and plenty of clothing. Share what you took from your enemies with your brothers.”
Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh left the other Israelites at Shiloh in Canaan and went back toward Gilead, the land they'd received as their own under the LORD's command through Moses.
When they reached the region near the Jordan in Canaan, Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh built an altar there by the river. It was big enough to make people stop and look.
The Israelites heard the news: “Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh have built an altar on the border of Canaan near the Jordan, on the side that belongs to Israel.”
When they heard, the whole Israelite community gathered at Shiloh to go to war against them.
The Israelites sent Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh in Gilead.
Ten leaders went with him, one from each tribe of Israel. Each was the head of his family among the clans of Israel.
They arrived in Gilead and spoke to the people of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.
“The whole community of the LORD asks, ‘Why have you broken faith with the God of Israel? Why have you turned away from following the LORD today by building your own altar and rebelling against him?
Wasn't the sin at Peor enough for us? We still haven't cleansed ourselves from it, even after a plague struck the LORD's community.
Are you really going to turn away from following the LORD today? If you rebel against the LORD today, tomorrow he'll be angry with the whole community of Israel.

If the land you received is unclean, cross into the LORD's own land, where his tabernacle stands, and take land among us. Don't rebel against the LORD or against us by building an altar besides the altar of the LORD our God.
Didn't Achan, a descendant of Zerah, break faith by taking what had been set apart? Anger fell on the whole community of Israel. Achan wasn't the only one who died because of his sin.’”
The people of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh answered the leaders of Israel's clans.
“The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows, and Israel will know. If we rebelled or broke faith with the LORD, don't save us today.
If we built this altar to turn away from the LORD, or to offer burnt offerings, grain offerings, or peace offerings on it, may the LORD himself hold us accountable.
We did this because we were worried that one day your children might ask ours, ‘What do you have to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?
The LORD made the Jordan a border between us and you people of Reuben and Gad. You have no share in the LORD.’ Then your children might make our children stop honoring the LORD.
So we said, ‘Let's build an altar, for a purpose other than burnt offerings or sacrifices.

It will serve as a witness between us and you, and between our descendants. It will show that we have a right to worship the LORD in his presence with our burnt offerings, sacrifices, and peace offerings.’ That way your children can't tell ours one day, ‘You have no share in the LORD.’

We thought, ‘If they ever say that to us or our descendants, we can answer, “Look at this copy of the LORD's altar that our ancestors made. It was built as a witness between us and you, with no burnt offerings or sacrifices made on it.”’

We would never rebel against the LORD or turn away from following him today by building an altar for burnt offerings, grain offerings, or sacrifices besides the altar of the LORD our God in front of his tabernacle!”
When Phinehas the priest and the leaders of Israel's clans with him heard what the people of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh said, they were satisfied.

Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest told the people of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh, “Today we know the LORD is among us, because you haven't broken faith with him in this. You've saved the Israelites from the LORD's hand.”
Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest and the leaders left Reuben and Gad in Gilead, went back to the Israelites in Canaan, and told them what had happened.
The Israelites were glad and blessed God. They stopped talking about going to war against Reuben and Gad or destroying the land where they lived.
The people of Reuben and Gad named the altar “A Witness Between Us That the LORD Is God.”
A long time after the LORD gave Israel rest from the enemies around them, Joshua was very old.
Joshua summoned all Israel, including the elders, leaders, judges, and officers, and told them, “I'm well along in years now.
You've seen everything the LORD your God did to these nations for your sake. The LORD your God fought for you.
I've assigned your tribes the land of the nations that remain, along with those I defeated, as your inheritance from the Jordan all the way west to the great sea.
The LORD your God will push them back and drive them out before you. You'll take possession of their land, just as he promised.
So be very brave and carefully follow everything written in the book of the law of Moses. Don't turn away from it to the right or to the left.
Don't mix with the nations that remain among you. Don't invoke the names of their gods, swear by them, serve them, or bow down to them.
Hold on to the LORD your God, as you've done to this day.
The LORD has driven out great and powerful nations ahead of you. To this day nobody has been able to stand against you.
One of you will chase a thousand, because the LORD your God is the one fighting for you, just as he promised.
So take care to love the LORD your God.
But if you turn back, attach yourselves to the survivors of these nations among you, and intermarry and mix with them,

you can be sure the LORD your God will stop driving these nations out ahead of you. They'll become a snare and a trap for you, lashes against your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from this good land the LORD your God gave you.
I'm about to go the way everyone on earth goes. You know with all your heart and soul that every good promise the LORD your God made about you has come true. Every single one.
Just as every good thing the LORD your God promised has come to you, he'll bring all the disasters he spoke of on you until he wipes you from this good land he gave you,

if you break the covenant the LORD your God commanded you to keep and go serve and bow down to other gods. Then the LORD's anger will burn against you, and you'll quickly perish from the good land he gave you.”
Joshua gathered all Israel's tribes at Shechem. He called the elders, leaders, judges, and officers, and they presented themselves before God.
Joshua told everyone, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘Long ago your ancestors lived across the Euphrates, including Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor. They served other gods.
I took your ancestor Abraham from across the river, led him through all of Canaan, and gave him many descendants. I gave him Isaac.
I gave Isaac two sons, Jacob and Esau. I gave Esau Mount Seir as his own, while Jacob and his children went down to Egypt.
I sent Moses and Aaron, struck Egypt with plagues, and then brought you out.
I brought your ancestors out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. The Egyptians chased your ancestors to the Red Sea with chariots and horsemen.

When your ancestors cried out to the LORD, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians. He brought the sea over them and covered them. You saw for yourselves what I did in Egypt. Then you lived in the wilderness a long time.
I brought you into the land of the Amorites across the Jordan. They fought you, and I handed them over to you. You took their land, and I destroyed them ahead of you.
Then Balak son of Zippor, the king of Moab, rose up to fight Israel. He sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse you.
I refused to listen to Balaam, so he kept blessing you, and I rescued you from his hand.

You crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho. The people of Jericho fought you, along with the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites. I handed them over to you.
I sent the hornet ahead of you to drive them out, including the two Amorite kings. It didn't take your sword or your bow.
I gave you land you hadn't worked and towns you hadn't built. You live in them now, and you eat from vineyards and olive groves you never planted.’
So honor the LORD and serve him sincerely and faithfully. Get rid of the gods your ancestors served across the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD.

If serving the LORD seems wrong to you, choose today whom you'll serve. Will it be the gods your ancestors served across the river or the gods of the Amorites whose land you live in? As for me and my household, we'll serve the LORD.”
The people answered, “We would never abandon the LORD to serve other gods!

The LORD our God brought us and our ancestors out of slavery in Egypt. He did those great signs right before our eyes and protected us along the whole journey and among all the peoples we passed through.
The LORD drove out all those peoples ahead of us, including the Amorites who lived here. So we'll serve the LORD too, because he's our God.”
Joshua told the people, “You can't serve the LORD, because he's a holy God and a jealous God. He won't forgive your rebellion and sins.
If you abandon the LORD and serve foreign gods, he'll turn against you, bring disaster on you, and destroy you after all the good he's done for you.”
The people answered Joshua, “No, we will serve the LORD.”
Joshua said, “You're witnesses against yourselves that you chose the LORD for yourselves and chose to serve him.” They answered, “We are witnesses.”
“Then get rid of the foreign gods among you and turn your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel.”
The people told Joshua, “We'll serve the LORD our God and listen to his voice.”
That day Joshua made a covenant with the people at Shechem and gave them a law and a ruling to live by.
Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God. He took a large stone and set it up under the oak by the LORD's sanctuary.
Joshua told everyone, “Look at this stone. It'll be a witness against us because it heard everything the LORD said to us. It'll testify against you if you deny your God.”
Then Joshua sent everyone home to their own inheritance.
After these things, Joshua son of Nun, the LORD's servant, died at 110 years old.
They buried him within his own land at Timnathserah in Ephraim's hill country, north of Mount Gaash.
Israel served the LORD throughout Joshua's life and throughout the lives of the elders who outlived him and knew everything the LORD had done for Israel.

The Israelites buried Joseph's bones, which they'd brought out of Egypt, at Shechem, in the plot Jacob had bought for a hundred pieces of silver from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem. That plot became the inheritance of Joseph's descendants.
Eleazar son of Aaron died, and they buried him on the hill belonging to his son Phinehas, which had been given to him in Ephraim's hill country.
